A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research on random dropping and over-squashing, with matching core sensitivity results. All 24 pages of v1 and 34 pages of v2, including appendices, support comparison despite substantial additions and reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original node-classification experiments, sensitivity simulations, and a ResGCN influence analysis in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 reports original sensitivity simulations, synthetic regression and real-world classification experiments, and evaluations of the newly proposed DropSens method.

M1.justification: v1 analyzes existing dropping methods without proposing a replacement. v2 introduces DropSens: incoming-edge dropping probabilities depend on the receiving node's degree and a prescribed fraction of preserved expected message weight, with probability clipping and an approximate solution (Section 4; Appendix E.3).

E1.justification: v2 adds SyntheticZINC regression, PubMed and Actor node classification, and graph classification on Mutag, Proteins, Enzymes, Reddit-Binary, IMDb-Binary and Collab. Proteins appeared in v1 only in sensitivity simulations. The additional datasets surveyed in Appendix A.2 are not all experimentally evaluated.

E2.justification: SkipNode, evaluated in v1 Table 2, disappears from v2's comparisons. v2 adds DropSens comparisons against fully adjacent layers, DIGL, SDRF, FoSR, GTR and undirected variants (Tables 2 and 8). Table 2 explicitly imports comparator scores from prior papers rather than reporting new baseline runs.

E3.justification: The primary evaluation shifts from correlations across dropping probabilities to comparisons of selected dropout configurations against NoDrop. Reported real-world training changes from learning rate 0.003 and weight decay 0.0005 to 0.001 and no weight decay. New protocols include 11-layer SyntheticZINC regression with MAE and a two-parameter DropSens search.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled information-mixing experiments, direct Monte Carlo influence comparisons in nonlinear GCNs, and an exact-versus-approximate DropSens probability analysis. Existing propagation-matrix analyses switch from Proteins to Cora. The underfitting investigation survives in Appendix F.3, but v1's ResGCN influence study and homophilic probability-sweep panels are removed.

E5.justification: v1 reports five runs per configuration and probability–accuracy correlations. v2 reports 20 runs for configuration selection and 30 additional runs for final 50-sample comparisons, adding one-sided t-tests, normality checks, power calculations and Hedges' g. Appendix F also adds error bars, although their meaning is not specified in the captions.

E6.justification: v1's correlation table is replaced by accuracy differences, synthetic MAEs, effect sizes and rewiring-comparison results. For example, v2 Table 2 reports DropSens at 53.01% versus SDRF plus Undirected at 44.46% on Chameleon, but 22.38% versus SDRF at 28.42% on Actor. These are newly reported comparisons, not same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: The central sensitivity lemmas, theorem, proofs and nonlinear extensions are retained, with substantial relocation. v2 adds the DropSens retained-information equation and its approximate solution, corrects the linear Monte Carlo propagation expression, and changes Appendix D.2's erroneous equality to an upper-bound inequality.

C1.justification: v2 expands the central contribution from diagnosing edge-dropping failures to proposing a sensitivity-preserving remedy and claiming superiority over graph-rewiring methods. The abstract and introduction also foreground feature/message dropout and synthetic and graph-level tasks. These materially broaden the paper's claims beyond v1's diagnostic focus.

C2.justification: v2 introduces the interpretation that graph-level pooling may reduce over-squashing's impact, explicitly questions homophily as a task-range proxy, and discusses potentially loose sensitivity bounds. It adds architecture-specific limitations of DropSens supported by poor GIN results, while removing v1's GraphSAGE/ResGCN extrapolation. The local-overfitting explanation is retained.

D1.justification: Appendix E adds hardware specifications, dataset splits, synthetic-data construction, readout details, learning-rate scheduling, DropSens parameter searches and a Python implementation. Table 9 records selected configurations. These substantially expand reproducibility information, although v1's explicit failed-GAT-run exclusion thresholds are no longer documented.

R1.justification: v2 adds a substantial review of homophily bias in previous evaluations, including a dataset inventory and exceptions (Appendix A.2). New citations support expanded benchmarking, architectures, implementation and statistics. DropSens also changes the research positioning from critique of existing methods to an alternative compared with established rewiring techniques.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contributions and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Nonlinear theory and several experimental discussions move into reorganized appendices, while DropSens and the expanded evaluation become central sections. An appendix contents page and separate experimental-analysis sections considerably change navigation and narrative structure.

P2.justification: v2 redesigns Figure 1, adds synthetic-performance and DropSens plots, introduces several comparison and configuration tables, and replaces the correlation display with significance-colored accuracy tables. Probability-sweep figures are revised with error bars and fewer panels; the ResGCN figure disappears. The document also adopts a different title, heading and table layout.

improvement.justification: v1 relies chiefly on homophily proxies and correlations across dropping probabilities. v2 substantially strengthens the central evidence through controlled SyntheticZINC mixing experiments, selected-configuration comparisons against NoDrop, statistical analysis and a documented constructive method. The gain is tempered by overstated DropSens superiority: Table 2 contains clear losses and Table 8 shows poor GIN performance, contradicting the abstract's consistency claim. Nevertheless, the stronger experimental design and reproducibility address important weaknesses of v1.
